Issued at 434 PM CDT Thu Aug 13 2026

-- FORECAST CHANGES OF NOTE/BIG PICTURE COMMENTS/UNCERTAINTIES:
- No truly major changes to speak of versus previous issuance
  last night/early this morning. That being said, as was
  expected here 24 hours ago...high temps for especially Sunday-
  Tuesday have trended a bit warmer (and possibly not enough),
  as any highs only in the 70s would appear most favored
  possibly Sunday and mainly in our north. 

- The most pressing/obvious very-short-term issue is assessing
  severe storm potential late this afternoon/especially
  evening...with our MAIN concern for a few severe storms
  (mainly with a damaging wind threat) focused 9PM-1AM and
  mainly in the southwestern quadrant of our CWA (counties
  mainly along/west of Hwy 281 and along/west of Hwy 6. 

- Big picture overview of the upper air pattern through the next
  week: Our RELATIVELY consistent pattern over the next week
  (fairly consistent warm-but-not-overly hot temperatures and
  intermittent rain/thunderstorm chances) is very typical for
  this time of year when we reside along the periphery/interface
  between a large-scale upper level high/ridge centered to our
  south...and the primary upper jet stream centered to our
  north. Really the only thing that changes is the spacial
  orientation of the ridge...as these next few days we remain
  under mainly southwesterly flow aloft (upper high centered
  over the Mid-South/southeastern states)...which then
  transitions to more west-northwesterly flow especially Sunday-
  Wednesday as the upper ridge retrogrades back west into the
  Southern Plains (TX/OK) and eventually southwest (NM/AZ). 

-- 7-DAY FORECAST CHRONOLOGICAL RUNDOWN (through Thurs. Aug.
 20):
- CURRENT/RECENT WEATHER SCENE:
Briefly backing up to last night/early this morning, forecasts
from 24 hours ago were fairly "spot on" that a potentially-
severe convective complex would march across our northern
counties. However, we did not necessarily anticipate a
particularly-damaging (thankfully narrow) swath of at least
70-80+ MPH winds centered roughly along a line from Arcadia-
North Loup-Greeley that caused considerable tree/power line and
some structural damage. 

In the wake of last night's long-departed storm complex
(actually still ongoing over southern Indiana), today has thus
far been dry/uneventful, under variable sky cover ranging from
mainly mostly cloudy north...to partly cloudy central...to 
mostly sunny south. In the mid-upper levels, water vapor
satellite and short term model data confirm that we reside under
the aforementioned west-southwesterly flow aloft, with the next
low-amplitude shortwave trough/disturbance of interest gradually
headed our way out of eastern CO.

At the surface, it's another day with a fairly big temperature
gradient across the CWA, thanks to that same sharp, quasi-
stationary front draped in west-east fashion across northern KS.
To the north of this boundary, most of our CWA is realizing 
highs between the low 80s-low 90s, in the presence of 
northeasterly/easterly breezes generally 10-15 MPH. However,
along and especially south of the boundary, temps in the mid-
upper 90s (and even limited 100+ extreme south) are present in
our KS counties. This same southern part of our CWA is also the
only area realizing 100+ heat index through early this
evening...with fairly widespread values of at least 100-105 and
possibly even localized up to ~ 110 (mainly Mitchell County).
As a result, a Heat Advisory continues in our KS counties until
9 PM. 


- LATE THIS AFTERNOON-OVERNIGHT:
As of this writing, a few "blips" of high-based convection are
just starting to develop about 30 miles south of our extreme
southeastern CWA (Lincoln County KS area)...in an area of very
steep low-level lapse rates/deep mixing south of the sharp
surface front. Leaning on higher-res models such as HRRR, at
some point mainly 5-8 PM could at least brush up into especially
Mitchell County in our extreme southeast...possibly posing a
threat for mainly severe wind gusts. 

However, of much higher confidence and concern is that
convection just getting underway over southwestern/south central
KS will accelerate northward into mainly the southwestern 
quadrant of our CWA mainly 9PM-1AM, posing a risk for at least
localized severe gusts to ~ 65 MPH, and perhaps hail up to
around quarter size (hail being the lesser threat). Although we
are NOT expecting a repeat of last night's very intense/damaging
winds, these storms will have plentiful instability (at least
2000-3000 J/kg CAPE, but a limiting factor of only modest deep-
layer shear mainly no more than 30-35KT. However, higher-res
models clearly depict at least localized damaging wind
potential...especially if a robust outflow surge is able to
develop along the leading edge of this activity. While the main
severe storm threat should largely wane by 12-1 AM, our entire
